clinicalPearls: Cerebral cavernous malformations are low-flow, angiographically occult clusters of thin-walled sinusoidal vascular channels lacking intervening brain parenchyma.
They occur as sporadic solitary lesions, often associated with a coexisting developmental venous anomaly, or as an autosomal dominant familial form with multiple lesions.
Familial disease is caused by loss-of-function variants in KRIT1 (CCM1), CCM2 (malcavernin) or PDCD10 (CCM3), the last carrying a more aggressive phenotype.
Gradient-echo or susceptibility-weighted magnetic resonance imaging is the most sensitive modality, showing a popcorn or mulberry lesion with a haemosiderin rim and multiple small blooming foci.
Seizures are the commonest presentation, followed by focal neurological deficit and symptomatic haemorrhage; many lesions are found incidentally.
Rebleeding risk is highest in the months following a symptomatic haemorrhage and is greater for brainstem and deep lesions.
PDCD10-related disease is associated with numerous lesions, early symptomatic bleeding and an increased frequency of associated brain tumours.
Management balances surgical resection of accessible symptomatic lesions against conservative surveillance for deep, brainstem or asymptomatic lesions.
reference.pathophysiology: Cerebral cavernous malformations are mulberry-like collections of dilated, thin-walled capillary-venous sinusoids lined by a single layer of endothelium with deficient tight junctions and absent intervening neural tissue, smooth muscle or elastic lamina. The familial form follows a two-hit mechanism in which a germline loss-of-function variant in one of the CCM genes is complemented by a somatic second hit within endothelial cells, so that lesions arise multifocally and accrue over time. The three CCM proteins, KRIT1, malcavernin and PDCD10, form an intracellular signalling complex that stabilises endothelial cell-cell junctions and restrains RhoA-ROCK and MEKK3-KLF signalling; disruption increases endothelial permeability, impairs junctional integrity and promotes aberrant angiogenesis. The fragile vessel walls leak chronically, depositing surrounding haemosiderin, and are prone to overt haemorrhage. Sporadic solitary lesions frequently coexist with a developmental venous anomaly, which is thought to create the local venous hypertension permitting cavernoma formation.
additionalDifferentials: Haemorrhagic metastasis or primary brain tumour
additionalInvestigations: Susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo magnetic resonance imaging to maximise lesion detection
Whole-neuraxis magnetic resonance imaging including spinal cord where familial disease is suspected
Molecular genetic testing of KRIT1, CCM2 and PDCD10 with cascade testing of relatives
Dermatological and, where indicated, retinal examination for associated cutaneous and retinal vascular lesions
Serial imaging surveillance to monitor lesion number and change
redFlags: Acute severe headache with new focal deficit suggesting symptomatic haemorrhage
Brainstem lesion producing cranial nerve palsy, ataxia or long-tract signs
Rapidly progressive or clustered new lesions raising concern for aggressive PDCD10 disease
New-onset or escalating seizures resistant to treatment
Signs of raised intracranial pressure from a large or bleeding lesion
reference.prognosis: Many cavernous malformations remain asymptomatic or cause well-controlled epilepsy, but symptomatic haemorrhage, particularly from brainstem or deep lesions, carries a meaningful risk of persistent neurological deficit and recurrent bleeding, with familial PDCD10 disease behaving most aggressively.
pitfalls: Relying on catheter angiography, on which these low-flow lesions are typically occult
Missing multiplicity because standard sequences under-detect small lesions compared with susceptibility-weighted imaging
Failing to recognise a familial pattern and offer genetic testing when multiple lesions are present
Overestimating the haemorrhage benefit of resecting deep or brainstem lesions against operative risk
Attributing all lesions to sporadic disease and overlooking an underlying developmental venous anomaly that must be preserved at surgery
references: International guidelines on cerebral cavernous malformation management
management: Manage asymptomatic or incidental lesions conservatively with serial MRI surveillance
Control seizures, the commonest presentation, with antiseizure medication
Offer microsurgical resection for accessible symptomatic lesions causing recurrent haemorrhage or drug-resistant epilepsy
Consider stereotactic radiosurgery for selected surgically inaccessible lesions where the evidence is limited
Take a cautious approach to antithrombotic therapy given the haemorrhage risk, especially for brainstem and deep lesions
Arrange genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives for familial KRIT1, CCM2 or PDCD10 disease, with whole-neuraxis imaging
Refer to neurosurgery or neurology and counsel on the higher rebleed risk in the months after a symptomatic haemorrhage
